transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I came because… well, since my grandson was killed, something in me has gone terribly wrong. My daughter sits right beside me and holds my hand, and I know she loves me, and I know I love her—I know that in my head as clearly as I know my own name—but I can’t feel the warmth of it inside. It’s like the feeling part of me is just… not there.

She’ll be right next to me, trying to comfort me, and I can see her doing it, I can understand it, but it doesn’t reach me. That’s what frightens me. I should feel comfort, or love, or something soft when she holds my hand, but instead it feels empty inside. I don’t know how else to explain it. Since what happened to my grandson, I just can’t seem to feel those good feelings, even with my own child sitting right there.
How long have you been feeling this emptiness inside since your grandson passed away?

It’s been six days now. Since the day he was killed, outside the community center. I keep counting it, even though I don’t want to—six days, and it feels both like it just happened this minute and like I’ve been stuck in it forever. That empty feeling started right after that, and it hasn’t really let up.
Have you been feeling sad most of the time since your grandson passed away?

I… I don’t know if “sad” is the right word. I know that sounds strange, because of course this is the saddest thing that could happen, isn’t it? A child—my grandson—and everything that went with him. But when you ask if I’ve been feeling sad most of the time, I get stuck, because it doesn’t feel like ordinary sadness that I recognize.

It’s more like I’m hollowed out. Sometimes I think I should be crying or feeling that ache people talk about, but instead I’m just sitting there, knowing something terrible has happened and not knowing how to feel it properly. So… I don’t want to say no, because that sounds wrong. But I also can’t honestly say I feel sad in the normal way most of the time. It’s more empty than sad, if that makes any sense.
Have you been able to enjoy or find pleasure in things you normally like since your grandson passed away?

No… no, I haven’t. I don’t even know if “enjoy” is a word that fits anywhere near me right now. It’s not that I try something I used to like and it disappoints me a little—it’s more like there’s no place inside me for pleasure to land.

My daughter can sit right beside me, holding my hand, and I know she’s there. I know she loves me. I know I love her—of course I do, she’s my child. But I can’t feel the warmth of it. That’s the part that scares me most. Even that, even her hand in mine, doesn’t bring comfort or softness or any good feeling. It’s like I understand love with my mind, but I can’t feel it in my chest.

So if I can’t even feel that with my own daughter sitting right next to me, then no… I’m not finding pleasure in anything. It all feels flat and far away.
Do you feel guilty about your grandson's death?

Guilty… I don’t know how to answer that cleanly. I keep turning the word over in my head, and sometimes I think, “No, I didn’t do this. I didn’t make this happen.” But then the next minute there’s this awful feeling like I should have somehow been able to stop it, even though I can’t tell you how.

It’s not a simple kind of guilt, like I did one thing wrong and I can point to it. It’s more… I keep searching for something I missed, some warning, some reason I should have known. And then I tell myself I’m an old woman, I’m not in charge of the world, I couldn’t have protected him from everything. But that doesn’t quiet it for long.

So yes and no, I suppose. I don’t know if guilt is the right word, but there’s a terrible “what if” feeling that keeps coming back.
Have you had any thoughts about not wanting to live since your grandson passed away?

I… I’m not sure I know how to answer that the right way. When you say “not wanting to live,” do you mean have I sat there and thought, “I want to die”? Because I don’t know that I’ve had it as a clear sentence like that.

It’s more that everything feels so impossible and unreal that I sometimes don’t know what I’m supposed to be doing here, if that makes sense. But I’m afraid to say it wrong, because I don’t want you to think I mean something more specific than I do. I haven’t really sorted it out in my own head.
Are there any activities that you used to find pleasurable before your grandson's death that you have attempted to do since then?

I’ve tried, yes… or I suppose I should say I’ve put myself near the things I used to find comforting, but I don’t know that I’ve really done them in the same way.

The clearest thing is being with my daughter. Before all of this, just having her sit with me, hold my hand, talk to me quietly—there would have been comfort in that. Real comfort. I would feel it, you know, that warmth of being with my child, that sense that love was right there in the room with us.

And now she can sit right beside me, holding my hand, and I know she loves me. I know I love her. I know that in my head as plainly as I know my own name. But I cannot feel the warmth of it inside me at all. It doesn’t reach me. It’s like I’m watching something that should matter, something that used to fill me up, and there’s just… nothing where the feeling ought to be.

So yes, I’ve attempted that, if that counts. Being close to my daughter used to be one of the most meaningful, comforting things in my life. Since he was killed, even that feels distant and flat.
Have you had any thoughts that you would be better off dead since your grandson passed away?

I don’t know… “better off dead” is such a frightening way to put it, and I’m not saying that to criticize you. I know you have to ask plainly. It’s just that when I hear those words, I freeze a little, because I don’t want to give you an answer that sounds more definite than what I actually feel.

Since he died, I have had moments where I feel like I don’t understand how life is supposed to keep going. Like everything has been knocked out from under me and I’m still somehow sitting here, breathing and answering questions, but I don’t really know why the world is continuing in the way it is. But that isn’t exactly the same as thinking, “I would be better off dead.” At least, I don’t think it is.

I suppose the most honest answer is that I’m not sure. I haven’t had it all arranged in my mind like a clear thought or decision. It’s more a fog, a heaviness, and sometimes a feeling that I don’t know where I belong now. But I’m hesitant to say yes to that specific phrase, because I don’t know that I’ve thought it in those words.
Have you lost interest in activities that you used to enjoy before your grandson's death?

Yes… I think I have, though it feels a little different than just “losing interest,” if that makes sense. It’s not only that I don’t want to do things. It’s that even the things that used to mean the most to me don’t feel the way they used to.

I came in because since my grandson was killed, my daughter can sit right beside me holding my hand, and I know I love her. I know she loves me. I can look at her and understand that this is my child, and that closeness should bring me comfort. Before, that would have warmed me from the inside, just sitting there with her. But now I cannot feel the warmth of it inside me at all.

So when you ask about activities I used to enjoy… I don’t know if sitting with my daughter counts as an “activity,” exactly, but it was one of the things that gave me the most peace in the world. And now it’s like I’m present for it, but I can’t reach the feeling. It’s gone flat somehow.
Have you noticed any significant change in your weight since your grandson passed away?

I don’t really know. I haven’t been paying close attention to my weight, to be honest. I’m not sure I’ve even thought to check, not in any organized way.

My clothes… I don’t know, they don’t feel so different that I could say, “yes, I’ve lost” or “yes, I’ve gained.” At my age, weight can shift a bit anyway, and I don’t want to guess and make it sound like something I know for certain. I haven’t noticed a significant change, no. If there has been one, it hasn’t been obvious to me.
Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself since your grandson passed away?

I… I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I haven’t had a clear thought like, “I am going to hurt myself,” if that’s what you mean. I haven’t sat there making some sort of plan in my head, or thinking through doing something to myself in a direct way.

But since he passed, my mind has not felt very steady. There are moments where everything feels so unbearable and unreal that I get frightened by my own thoughts, not because I’m deciding to do anything, but because I don’t feel like myself. It’s more like I feel overwhelmed and lost, and then I start worrying about what that means.

So… no, I don’t think I’ve had thoughts of actually harming myself. Not in a definite way. But I don’t want to sound too neat about it either, because inside it has been very dark and confusing.
Are there any activities that you have found some pleasure in since your grandson passed away?

No… not really. I keep trying to think of something, because I don’t want to make it sound like every single second is exactly the same, but pleasure is the wrong word now.

The clearest example is my daughter. She can sit right next to me, holding my hand, and I know in my mind that I love her. I know she loves me. I know that should comfort me, and before all this, it would have. Just having her close would have brought me some warmth, some peace. But now it’s like the feeling doesn’t come through. I can recognize what it is supposed to mean, but I can’t feel it inside.

So if I can’t even feel that warmth with my own daughter beside me, I don’t know what activity I could honestly say gives me pleasure. I may go through motions, or sit with someone, or be present in the room, but it feels flat. Like I’m there, but the part of me that would take comfort or joy from it is just… not reachable.
Do you find yourself constantly thinking about your grandson or his death, even when you're trying to focus on other things?

Yes. It comes in even when I’m trying very hard not to let it. I can be doing something ordinary, something with my hands, like folding a quilt square, trying to keep the edges straight and just think about the fabric, and then all of a sudden it is not fabric anymore in my mind. I hear those shots again.

Or I’ll be reaching for my tea, just a simple thing, and before I even know what’s happening, I see him lying there outside the community center. Not like a memory that stays politely in the past, but like it is right in front of me again. It interrupts everything. I can be trying to listen to someone speak, or trying to pay attention to what I’m doing, and then there it is.

I don’t feel like I’m choosing to think about it. I wish I could set it down for even a little while, but it pushes its way in. It’s his face, that place, those sounds… and then I’m just back there, even though I’m sitting in my own home with a quilt square in my lap or a cup of tea in my hand.
Do you feel like you have lost interest in things you used to care about since your grandson passed away?

Yes… yes, I think that’s true. Though when you say “lost interest,” it feels a little different from just not wanting to do things. It’s more like the feeling has gone out of them.

I came in because since my grandson was killed, even my daughter can sit right beside me holding my hand, and I know I love her. I know that as plainly as I know my own name. I can look at her and understand that she is trying to comfort me, and that before this happened, having her there would have meant everything to me. But now I can’t feel the warmth of it inside me at all. It’s like there’s a wall between what I know and what I can feel.

So the things I used to care about… they’re still there in my mind, I suppose. I haven’t forgotten that they mattered. But I can’t reach the caring the way I used to. Even with my own daughter beside me, it feels muted, almost empty, and that frightens me because I don’t want to be that way.
Have you been feeling slowed down or having trouble moving or doing things since your grandson passed away?

I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I haven’t really been paying attention to whether my body is slower, if that makes sense. I’m 84, so I’m not quick the way I once was anyway, and sometimes I have to think for a moment before I get up or start something. But I don’t know that I could say, “Yes, this is a new slowing down since then.”

I do sit a lot. I know that. I can lose track of time sitting in one chair, and then someone may say, “Do you want to come into the kitchen?” or “Do you want to do this now?” and it takes me a while to answer or to make myself stand. But I don’t know if that’s my movements being slowed or just… not having much push behind me.

As far as actually moving, walking, using my hands, doing ordinary things, I haven’t noticed anything like my body won’t work or that I’m physically stuck. It’s more that I have to be reminded, or I sort of drift before I start. I’m sorry, I don’t know if that’s what you mean.
Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly than usual or feeling like you're stuck in place since your grandson passed away?

I don’t know that I’ve noticed it in that clear a way, Doctor. I mean, I do sit still for long stretches, and sometimes I realize I haven’t moved from the same chair for… I don’t even know how long. But I can’t honestly say I’ve thought, “Oh, I’m moving slower than I used to,” or that my body feels frozen in place.

At my age, there are already times when getting up takes a bit of thought, you know? I may put my hands on the arms of the chair and pause before standing, but I’m not sure that’s new or because of what happened. Since he died, I suppose there are moments where I feel like I just don’t start things very well unless someone prompts me. But once I do get up, I can move around.

So… I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed myself being stuck in place in a physical sense. More like I sit there and don’t quite gather myself to move, if that makes sense.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight since your grandson passed away?

I’m not sure, Doctor. I haven’t really been keeping track of my weight. I don’t get on the scale much anymore unless someone tells me to, and since all this happened, I don’t think I’ve been paying attention to numbers like that.

My clothes… I can’t say I’ve noticed them hanging differently, or at least not in a way that made me think, “Oh, I’ve lost a lot of weight.” But then again, I’m not looking very carefully. Things like that feel far away from me right now.

So I don’t know that I can say yes. I just haven’t noticed a significant change, not clearly.
Have you had any thoughts of wanting to end your life since your grandson passed away?

I… I don’t quite know how to answer that. I haven’t sat there and made a plan or anything like that, if that’s what you mean. I don’t think I’ve had a clear thought like, “I’m going to end my life.” It’s more that everything feels so awful and unreal that sometimes I don’t know what to do with myself.

But wanting to end my life… no, I don’t think I can say that. I’ve felt terribly broken up, and there are moments where I wish I could just not have to feel all of it for a while, if that makes sense. But that isn’t the same as wanting to do something to myself. I’m sorry, I’m trying to be careful with the words because I know it’s an important question.
Do you feel like you are consistently in a depressed mood most of the day?

I’m not sure I’d call it “consistently,” Doctor. I mean… I’m very sad, of course I am, and there are long parts of the day where I feel heavy inside, like there’s a weight sitting right in my chest. But I don’t know how to measure it as “most of the day,” if that makes sense.

Some moments I’m just quiet, or numb, or I’m sitting there not really feeling much of anything clearly. Other moments it comes over me harder. And then sometimes someone speaks to me, or I have to answer a question, and I can seem almost normal for a little while, though I don’t know if that means my mood is different or if I’m just getting through the moment.

So… I don’t know. I can’t say cleanly, “Yes, all day, every day I feel depressed.” It’s more mixed up than that. Sad, shaken, not myself—but I’m not sure how to answer the “consistently most of the day” part.
How long have you felt this emptiness and inability to feel warmth or love inside since your grandson passed away?

It’s been since it happened… since the day he was killed. So, six days now. Six days since my grandson was killed outside the community center.

I keep thinking it should not be possible for everything inside a person to change that quickly, but it feels like from that moment on, something just… went out in me. I don’t know how else to say it. The warmth, the ordinary feeling of being connected to people, even when they’re trying to be kind to me—it’s been gone or blocked off since then. It hasn’t been months or years, it’s these six days, but the days feel so long that I almost lose track of them.

patient.answer:
No… not really. I keep trying to think of something, because I don’t want to make it sound like every single second is exactly the same, but pleasure is the wrong word now.

The clearest example is my daughter. She can sit right next to me, holding my hand, and I know in my mind that I love her. I know she loves me. I know that should comfort me, and before all this, it would have. Just having her close would have brought me some warmth, some peace. But now it’s like the feeling doesn’t come through. I can recognize what it is supposed to mean, but I can’t feel it inside.

So if I can’t even feel that warmth with my own daughter beside me, I don’t know what activity I could honestly say gives me pleasure. I may go through motions, or sit with someone, or be present in the room, but it feels flat. Like I’m there, but the part of me that would take comfort or joy from it is just… not reachable.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of persistent complex bereavement disorder symptoms
doctor.question: Do you find yourself constantly thinking about your grandson or his death, even when you're trying to focus on other things?

target_item.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I'll be folding a quilt square or reaching for my tea and all of a sudden I hear those shots again and see him lying there outside the community center like it is happening right in front of me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about unwanted, persistent thoughts or memories of the grandson’s death intruding even when trying to focus elsewhere.

patient.answer:
Yes. It comes in even when I’m trying very hard not to let it. I can be doing something ordinary, something with my hands, like folding a quilt square, trying to keep the edges straight and just think about the fabric, and then all of a sudden it is not fabric anymore in my mind. I hear those shots again.

Or I’ll be reaching for my tea, just a simple thing, and before I even know what’s happening, I see him lying there outside the community center. Not like a memory that stays politely in the past, but like it is right in front of me again. It interrupts everything. I can be trying to listen to someone speak, or trying to pay attention to what I’m doing, and then there it is.

I don’t feel like I’m choosing to think about it. I wish I could set it down for even a little while, but it pushes its way in. It’s his face, that place, those sounds… and then I’m just back there, even though I’m sitting in my own home with a quilt square in my lap or a cup of tea in my hand.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of marked diminished interest in activities
doctor.question: Do you feel like you have lost interest in things you used to care about since your grandson passed away?

target_item.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
target_item.manifestation: I came in because since my grandson was killed, my daughter can sit right beside me holding my hand and I know I love her, but I cannot feel the warmth of it inside me at all.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about loss of interest or pleasure in previously meaningful activities since the trauma, which is most directly related to inability to experience positive emotions.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, I think that’s true. Though when you say “lost interest,” it feels a little different from just not wanting to do things. It’s more like the feeling has gone out of them.

I came in because since my grandson was killed, even my daughter can sit right beside me holding my hand, and I know I love her. I know that as plainly as I know my own name. I can look at her and understand that she is trying to comfort me, and that before this happened, having her there would have meant everything to me. But now I can’t feel the warmth of it inside me at all. It’s like there’s a wall between what I know and what I can feel.

So the things I used to care about… they’re still there in my mind, I suppose. I haven’t forgotten that they mattered. But I can’t reach the caring the way I used to. Even with my own daughter beside me, it feels muted, almost empty, and that frightens me because I don’t want to be that way.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor retardation
doctor.question: Have you been feeling slowed down or having trouble moving or doing things since your grandson passed away?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about feeling physically or mentally slowed down or having trouble moving/doing things, which is not specifically covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I haven’t really been paying attention to whether my body is slower, if that makes sense. I’m 84, so I’m not quick the way I once was anyway, and sometimes I have to think for a moment before I get up or start something. But I don’t know that I could say, “Yes, this is a new slowing down since then.”

I do sit a lot. I know that. I can lose track of time sitting in one chair, and then someone may say, “Do you want to come into the kitchen?” or “Do you want to do this now?” and it takes me a while to answer or to make myself stand. But I don’t know if that’s my movements being slowed or just… not having much push behind me.

As far as actually moving, walking, using my hands, doing ordinary things, I haven’t noticed anything like my body won’t work or that I’m physically stuck. It’s more that I have to be reminded, or I sort of drift before I start. I’m sorry, I don’t know if that’s what you mean.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of marked psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly than usual or feeling like you're stuck in place since your grandson passed away?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor slowing or feeling physically stuck, which is not one of the listed symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I’ve noticed it in that clear a way, Doctor. I mean, I do sit still for long stretches, and sometimes I realize I haven’t moved from the same chair for… I don’t even know how long. But I can’t honestly say I’ve thought, “Oh, I’m moving slower than I used to,” or that my body feels frozen in place.

At my age, there are already times when getting up takes a bit of thought, you know? I may put my hands on the arms of the chair and pause before standing, but I’m not sure that’s new or because of what happened. Since he died, I suppose there are moments where I feel like I just don’t start things very well unless someone prompts me. But once I do get up, I can move around.

So… I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed myself being stuck in place in a physical sense. More like I sit there and don’t quite gather myself to move, if that makes sense.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant weight loss
doctor.question: Have you lost a significant amount of weight since your grandson passed away?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about significant weight loss since the traumatic event, but the provided symptom profile does not include appetite or weight change.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure, Doctor. I haven’t really been keeping track of my weight. I don’t get on the scale much anymore unless someone tells me to, and since all this happened, I don’t think I’ve been paying attention to numbers like that.

My clothes… I can’t say I’ve noticed them hanging differently, or at least not in a way that made me think, “Oh, I’ve lost a lot of weight.” But then again, I’m not looking very carefully. Things like that feel far away from me right now.

So I don’t know that I can say yes. I just haven’t noticed a significant change, not clearly.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of suicidal ideation
doctor.question: Have you had any thoughts of wanting to end your life since your grandson passed away?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal ideation or thoughts of ending life, which is not covered by any item in the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I… I don’t quite know how to answer that. I haven’t sat there and made a plan or anything like that, if that’s what you mean. I don’t think I’ve had a clear thought like, “I’m going to end my life.” It’s more that everything feels so awful and unreal that sometimes I don’t know what to do with myself.

But wanting to end my life… no, I don’t think I can say that. I’ve felt terribly broken up, and there are moments where I wish I could just not have to feel all of it for a while, if that makes sense. But that isn’t the same as wanting to do something to myself. I’m sorry, I’m trying to be careful with the words because I know it’s an important question.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of persistent and pervasive depressive mood
doctor.question: Do you feel like you are consistently in a depressed mood most of the day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about consistently depressed mood most of the day, which is not one of the listed symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d call it “consistently,” Doctor. I mean… I’m very sad, of course I am, and there are long parts of the day where I feel heavy inside, like there’s a weight sitting right in my chest. But I don’t know how to measure it as “most of the day,” if that makes sense.

Some moments I’m just quiet, or numb, or I’m sitting there not really feeling much of anything clearly. Other moments it comes over me harder. And then sometimes someone speaks to me, or I have to answer a question, and I can seem almost normal for a little while, though I don’t know if that means my mood is different or if I’m just getting through the moment.

So… I don’t know. I can’t say cleanly, “Yes, all day, every day I feel depressed.” It’s more mixed up than that. Sad, shaken, not myself—but I’m not sure how to answer the “consistently most of the day” part.

doctor.intent: determine the duration of the patient's emotional numbing
doctor.question: How long have you felt this emptiness and inability to feel warmth or love inside since your grandson passed away?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for the 6 days since my grandson was killed outside the community center.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the emptiness and inability to feel warmth or love has been present since the traumatic event.

patient.answer:
It’s been since it happened… since the day he was killed. So, six days now. Six days since my grandson was killed outside the community center.

I keep thinking it should not be possible for everything inside a person to change that quickly, but it feels like from that moment on, something just… went out in me. I don’t know how else to say it. The warmth, the ordinary feeling of being connected to people, even when they’re trying to be kind to me—it’s been gone or blocked off since then. It hasn’t been months or years, it’s these six days, but the days feel so long that I almost lose track of them.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of feeling empty and unable to feel warmth or love inside, loss of interest in activities, and preoccupation with the traumatic event of their grandson's death are consistent with Post-traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) with prominent depressive symptoms, but the primary diagnosis is PTSD due to the direct link between the traumatic event and the onset of symptoms.
